title: Percussion
objective: After this level you can explain how drums and other percussion instruments make sound.
summary: Percussion is idiophones and membranophones, mostly struck. Some is pitched (xylophone, timpani), some not (cymbals, snare). A tighter drumhead sounds higher.

cards.headline: Hit it, shake it, scrape it: that's percussion.
cards.body: Most percussion is struck, but some is shaken, scraped, rubbed or even plucked. That makes it the orchestra's most mixed-up family. Can a family of things you hit ever play a tune?

cards.headline: A skin, or the whole thing
cards.body: Use Level 11's rule. In percussion, two answers come up. On a drum, a stretched membrane vibrates: a membranophone. On a bell, a clapper or a rattle, the instrument's own body vibrates: an idiophone. Either way, the hit only starts things; the shaking surface does the work, pushing on the air like any other vibrating object.

cards.headline: Pitched and unpitched
cards.body: Some percussion plays definite notes: a xylophone or timpani can carry a melody. Others, like cymbals and snare drums, have no definite pitch; you can't hum back a cymbal crash. Even the pitched ones typically mark and push the rhythm, locking onto Level 4's steady pulse, the beat.

cards.headline: Tuning a drum
cards.body: A drumhead behaves a lot like Level 12's string: the tighter it's stretched, the higher it sounds. Timpani, the big kettledrums, use this to hit exact notes, and they're the only drums in a Western orchestra tuned to definite pitch. By the 16th century, screws around their copper shells tightened the heads. They're played in sets of two or more, each tuned to a different pitch; today's standard set has four.

cards.headline: Percussion: struck
learned: Pitched: xylophone, timpani; unpitched: cymbals, snare
Timpani: tuned drums, in sets of two or more

questions.prompt: Which of these percussion instruments plays definite pitches?

options.label: Cymbals
options.rationale: A cymbal crash has no definite pitch.

options.label: Snare drum
options.rationale: A snare drum has no definite pitch.

options.label: Rattle
options.rationale: A rattle is shaken for rhythm, not tuned to notes.

questions.explanation: Xylophones and timpani sound definite pitches; cymbals and snare drums don't.

questions.prompt: A timpanist tightens the head of a drum. What happens to its note?

options.label: It loses its pitch
options.rationale: Timpani keep a definite pitch as they are tuned.

questions.explanation: The tighter a drum's membrane is stretched, the higher its pitch, just like a string.

questions.prompt: Using Level 11's sorting rule, why is a drum a membranophone but a bell an idiophone?

options.label: A drum is louder than a bell
A bell is made of metal, a drum of wood
A drum is struck, while a bell is shaken
options.rationale: Both can be struck; the difference is what vibrates.

options.label: A drum's stretched skin vibrates; a bell's own body does

questions.explanation: The rule asks what vibrates: a drum's stretched membrane, but the whole body of a bell.
